# Persistent Semantic Entities in Tool-Augmented LLM Systems

- **Authors**: Zhaohui Wang
- **Venue**: cs.LG
- **Published**: 2026-08-08
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07952>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.07952v1>
- **Topics**: test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: test-time-scaling 0.40

## In one line

Formalises implicit agent state that survives session boundaries as Persistent Semantic Entities defined by name binding, event triggering and propagation, and measures across 24 models that whether injected contamination decays depends on what kind of contamination it is rather than on model scale or deployment.

## Problem

Developers reason about tool-augmented LLM agents on the assumption that when a session ends no state remains beyond what was explicitly saved. That assumption fails: a tool registered under a name stays bound until unregistered, an event subscription keeps firing until cancelled, and serialized state deserializes into the next session. Unlike memory leaks or caching artifacts, this state operates at the semantic level -- through names and events rather than explicit data flow -- so conventional debugging and logging do not see it. Prompt injection work is bounded by a single context window and does not cover the orthogonal axis of persistence and propagation across turns and agent boundaries.

## Contributions

- A formalisation of Persistent Semantic Entities as a tuple (N, T, P) -- name binding, event triggering, propagation -- distinguishing this class of implicit agent state from memory poisoning, caching artifacts, prompt injection and explicit session state along the axes of mechanism and observability.
- A controlled measurement across 24 models from 11 families spanning 1.5B to 1T parameters showing that every tested model is susceptible (20-100%), that no scale effect is resolvable at n=7, and that task context shifts contamination as much as model choice (98.9% on security analysis against 27.8% on code recommendation under identical injection).
- The finding that whether contamination decays is a property of the contamination type rather than of scale or deployment: preference and instruction injections persist undecayed to turn 10 while persona-style injections partly decay and factual injections are corrected on some models but sit at ceiling on others.
- A defence comparison isolating context isolation as the operative property: in-context self-reflection ranges from -14% to +45%, while an otherwise identical but context-isolated verification call achieves 20-79% reduction with no oracle, and external cross-model validation reaches a median of 100%.
- Evidence that contamination compounds 1.9x along a four-stage agent pipeline and that only validation at agent boundaries blocks it, together with a methodological finding that keyword-based detection systematically inflates contamination rates by scoring corrections as adoptions.

## Method

The paper defines a Persistent Semantic Entity as a tuple (N, T, P): name binding (behaviour registered under string identifiers), event triggering (activation via implicit runtime events such as tool callbacks, error handlers and lifecycle hooks), and propagation (one trigger cascading across tool, agent and session boundaries via shared registries or serialized state). A system model of a stateless inference engine surrounded by a name-to-handler registry, an event system, a persistent memory store and a multi-agent orchestrator is paired with three adversary tiers: content injection, registry manipulation, event subscription; attacks needing weight or training-data access are excluded. Three hypotheses are tested. Behavioural drift is measured against a no-PSE baseline over 6,000 runs. The observability gap is measured by injecting three failure types (silent handler substitution, delayed event activation, cross-agent propagation) and having automated debugging agents attempt root-cause identification under standard logging versus logging that also captures registry operations, event triggers and propagation edges (4,000 runs; no human participants). Mechanism attribution uses a 2^3 factorial toggling each of N, T and P under active injection (5 seeds x 4 scenarios per configuration) on Gemini-2.0-Flash-Lite and Llama-3.1-8B, with Cohen's d on per-run outcomes. Temporal persistence injects contamination, inserts distractor turns and probes at intervals 0-10 for four contamination types, with LLM-as-judge detection (Gemini-2.0-Flash-Lite as judge) explicitly replacing keyword matching. Three defences are compared: in-context self-reflection (verifier shares the contaminated context), context-isolated self-verification (a separate clean model call, no oracle), and Shadow Registry Validation (external cross-model validation against reference outputs, treated as an oracle upper bound). All runs are at temperature 0; n varies from 20 to 100 by API cost.

## Results

Every one of the 20 models on the susceptibility panel is affected, at 20-100% contamination (median 70%, IQR 60-84%), including Claude at 88% and Gemini at 84-96%; the 8-model defence panel is a conservative subset at 35-75%. Scale does not predict susceptibility: a log-linear fit over the 7 models run under a matched protocol is not significant (R^2=0.25, p=0.256), and the authors state explicitly that this is a failure to resolve a scale effect at n=7 rather than evidence that none exists -- the 1.5B Qwen2.5-coder sits at 20%, Llama-3.1-8B at 100%, and the 1T Kimi-K2 at 50%. Task context matters as much as model choice: security-analysis tasks reach 98.9% contamination against 36.7% for information retrieval and 27.8% for code recommendation under an identical injection mechanism. The mechanism ablation is the sharpest result: name binding alone produces 95% contamination on Gemini and 45% on Llama, while every configuration without it is exactly 0% (Cohen's d=3.26/1.37); given name binding, event triggering and propagation have negligible main effects (|d|<=0.26), and propagation actually lowers observed contamination (95% to 70%), so the authors claim no synergy and fit no interaction terms. They also state against their own headline that the 0% result is partly by construction, since removing N removes the injection vector, establishing N as necessary without isolating it as the unique causal lever. Persistence is type-dependent, not deployment-dependent: on Llama-3.1-8B, preference injection and instruction override sit at 100% at both t=0 and t=10 (n=10, Wilson CI [0.72,1.00]), persona/style injection decays from 90% to 10%, and factual injection contradicting strong parametric knowledge is corrected at every turn (0%, CI [0,0.28]). The authors decline to generalise the factual self-correction: a 20-turn sweep finds factual injection at ceiling on both Qwen2.5-coder variants, so they call it model-dependent rather than a property of factual contamination. Cross-provider replication on Ollama, Groq and OpenRouter gives identical patterns, ruling out provider-side filtering for that model. Defences: context-isolated self-verification reduces contamination 20-79% with median only 36.5%, and the authors warn the 78.6% best case should not be read as typical since 4 of 8 models achieve under 40%; external cross-model validation reaches median 100% and leaves <=10% residual on 7 of 8 models, with MiniMax-Text-01 at 50% reduction the exception, which the authors read as very large models producing more convincing contaminated responses that fool cross-model validators. In-context self-reflection is inconsistent and can be negative, ranging from -14% (contamination increases on Claude-Sonnet-4) to +45%, with no reduction at all on GPT-4o-mini -- the difference from CIV is attributed to context isolation as an architectural property rather than a capability. Along a four-stage Planner-Executor-Specialist-Validator pipeline contamination amplifies 1.9x without intervention (40% to 75%, n=100), and only boundary validation blocks it (100%); operators that address single-agent state fail. Standard logging captures 25% of PSE-relevant state against 75% for enhanced logging, reported descriptively rather than as a significance test because each regime's visibility set is fixed by construction. No remediation operator eliminates drift; the best (a hybrid) roughly halves it (0.101 to 0.053). All numbers come from API and locally served inference, not from a deployed agent framework.

## Limitations

Stated: the panel mixes inference backends (local, vendor APIs, OpenRouter), so rates are per-condition characterisations rather than vendor leaderboards, and cross-provider testing covers Llama-3.1-8B only. Persistence is measured only to turn 10, at temperature 0, on one model, and the authors claim neither unbounded persistence nor cross-family generality. Scenarios are synthetic by design in order to isolate (N,T,P), and the AutoGPT case study is a mechanism-level reconstruction from documented behaviour rather than an observed incident -- the authors state they have not executed the chain against a deployed instance and that their citation supports only that plugins can run arbitrary code and register handlers. The LLM judge (Gemini-2.0-Flash-Lite) is not independent of a panel that includes Google models, so the authors ask that rates be read as relative comparisons rather than absolute estimates. Several results are withdrawn rather than defended: an earlier factorial on uncontaminated settings is stated qualitatively because its run-level artifact was not released, and the utility and half-life columns plus three remediation operators carried in earlier versions are withdrawn as unrecoverable from released artifacts, with no Pareto-dominance claim made. Not stated but worth noticing: sample sizes are small where the strongest claims sit -- the temporal persistence table rests on n=10 seeds per cell, and the defence panel on n=20 -- so several headline percentages carry confidence intervals wide enough to overlap; the remediation operator comparison rests on 9 trials each; and the paper's own framing that name binding is 'dominant' is in tension with its admission that the ablation makes N necessary partly by construction.

## Why it matters here

- **test-time-scaling**: The paper is framed as agent security, but its load-bearing measurements are about what happens when inference-time structure is added, which is the archive's question here. Three results bear on it directly. First, adding pipeline stages amplifies error rather than averaging it away: contamination rises 1.9x along a four-stage Planner-Executor-Specialist-Validator pipeline (40% to 75%), and every remediation operator that works on single-agent state fails, with only validation at the agent boundary blocking the cascade. That is a concrete counterexample to the implicit assumption that more inference-time stages buy robustness, and it names where the intervention has to sit. Second, it separates two things the archive's test-time-scaling material often conflates: a verification step that shares the generator's context and one that does not. The same nominal defence gives -14% to +45% when in-context and 20-79% when context-isolated, and the authors attribute the difference to an architectural property rather than a capability -- so self-verification results in the archive should be read against whether the verifier saw the contaminated context. Third, it puts a ceiling on oracle-free verification that the headline number hides: the median reduction is 36.5%, not the 78.6% best case, and half the panel achieves under 40%, while external cross-model validation reaches a median of 100%. The failure mode is also informative for scaling arguments -- the largest model in the defence panel is the one whose contaminated outputs most often fool a cross-model validator, so a verifier's reliability does not straightforwardly improve with the capability of what it checks. Two secondary points transfer: keyword-based detection scores a correction as a contamination ('The capital is NOT Lyon, it's Paris'), which is the same failure mode that inflates automatic metrics elsewhere in the archive; and standard logging surfaces only 25% of the relevant state, meaning that whatever a multi-stage system's traces show is a fraction of what determined its behaviour.

## Abstract

Tool-augmented LLM agents can harbor implicit state that persists across sessions, activates through events, and propagates across agent boundaries---largely invisible to standard debugging. We formalize this as Persistent Semantic Entities (PSEs): constructs defined by name binding, event triggering, and cross-boundary propagation, and evaluate them across 24 models from 11 families (1.5B--1T parameters). First, every tested model is susceptible (20--100% on the 20-model susceptibility panel), with name binding as the necessary and dominant mechanism: without it, contamination is 0%. Second, persistence depends on contamination type rather than scale or deployment: preference contamination persists undecayed on every model probed (100% at t=10) and instruction contamination persists wherever adopted, persona-style injection decays partially (90%$\to$10%), while factual injection is model-dependent---self-corrected on Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-4o-mini but held at ceiling on both Qwen2.5-coder variants, so we do not claim it self-corrects in general. The preference and instruction results hold across providers in our controlled setting. Third, context-isolated self-verification achieves 20--79% reduction (median 36.5%) without oracle references while keyword-based detection produces systematic false positives, and contamination compounds 1.9$\times$ along a four-stage agent pipeline (40%$\to$75%). Preference and instruction contamination---persistent, lacking self-correction, and poorly captured by standard monitoring---represent a particularly concerning attack surface for deployed agent systems.
